transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-07
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Evan Cho (CTO, StrataGrid), Rhea Patel (Head of ML), Marcus Li (Infra Lead), Sofia Mendez (Product)

Auto-generated summary (may be rough):
- StrataGrid is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for inference of an energy forecasting model (1500 token average context, some 4k peaks).
- Primary constraints: monthly budget cap (~$25k), strict residency for certain telemetry, p99 latency target < 250ms for real-time alerts, preference to avoid heavy infra ops.

- per-token and embedding pricing math

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: hey thanks everyone for joining, uh we'll do quick intros and then jump to the cost stuff, is that fine?
[00:08] Evan: yep, that works for us. I'm Evan, CTO at StrataGrid. we run a forecasting ensemble, main inference workload is about 10k requests per hour, a lot of them short (250-500 tokens) but with bursts and some long runs for scenario sim, up to 4k tokens.
[00:27] Rhea: hi all I'm Rhea, I lead ML, the model is an open-ish transformer variant, we fine-tuned, and caching would help a lot on prefix-heavy reads.
[00:36] Jordan: great, Priya will walk through the batching and cache levers and then we can go into pricing math.
[00:42] Priya: hey! quick note, forgive any stutters, I was debugging a lab env. OK so two levers that materially change per-token: batching and prefix/KV caching. batching is basically grouping in-flight requests to amortize per-call overhead, so larger batch size lowers per-token cost but can increase latency.
[00:58] Marcus: so, when you say batch size, does that require us to change client side logic? we don't want to add complex buffering in the edge service.
[01:06] Priya: good question. you can do it transparently if you use our SDK with continuous batching -- it aggregates short windows (usually 20-200ms) so your code doesn't need to buffer, but if you want very predictable p99 you can set batching windows or go dedicated for more control.
[01:22] Rhea: and how about KV cache, we've got a lot of repeated prefixes for stateful sims — is that automatic or we have to configure something?
[01:30] Priya: KV cache is available in both hosted and dedicated. hosted has some shared cache tiers, dedicated gives you more guarantee and larger cache allocations, and private (VPC) can run an on-prem cache if needed. sometimes the auto-detection mislabels tokens - sorry the speech to text wrote K V cash earlier in the notes — but the idea is we store key-value hidden state to avoid recomputing.
[01:50] [Speaker 1]: mm-hmm
[01:52] Jordan: let's walk through an example math. Assume baseline generation 100 tokens per call, p50 latency target 120ms. On hosted, per-token price X (we'll share sheet) plus a call overhead Y. If you enable caching and get a 30% hit rate on prefixes, your effective per-token cost drops significantly.
[02:12] Evan: quick interruption — our finance owner set a monthly cap of $25k for pilot. we need an estimate for expected burn at 10k rph and average tokens.
[02:21] Luis: ok we can ballpark during this call and then run the real benchmark. rough calc: 10k rph * (avg 200 tokens) = 2M tokens/hour i think that math: wait, 10k requests per hour, *200 tokens = 2M tokens per hour yes, multiply by 24 ~48M tokens/day, sorry that seems high, let's re-evaluate.
[02:44] Rhea: I think the actual production QPS will be lower in realtime path, the 10k was batch/analytics included. our real-time alert path is ~600 rph.
[02:52] Priya: ok that's a big difference. so two lanes: realtime (600 rph, strict p99) and analytics (10k rph, tolerant latency). many customers separate those into different hosting mixes to control cost.
[03:06] Jordan: for the budget cap, a common pattern: host realtime on Dedicated (reserved capacity) to hit p99 SLAs and route analytics to Hosted capacity or even lower-cost quantized variants. dedicated gives predictable throughput pricing and lower per-token when committed.
[03:21] Marcus: how big of a reservation are we talking to get decent per-token economy? our infra team likes commitments but not big surprises.
[03:28] Priya: ballpark: for an LLM ~7B-ish architecture, committing to a small dedicated pool that handles your p99 QPS (say 8-12 tokens per GPU cycle) can cut per-token by 20-40% relative to on-demand hosted. exacts depend on sequence length distribution and quantization. we'll calculate with your prompt profile.
[03:47] Evan: data residency — some telemetry must remain in EU. can Redwood Hosted support region pinning?
[03:54] Jordan: yes, hosted has regional endpoints. but if you need strict control/air-gapped logs and customer-managed keys we usually recommend Private (VPC/on-prem) or Dedicated with VPC peering and KMS.
[04:06] Rhea: and for SOC2 / audit logs we need detailed per-request traces and retention for 365 days. is that possible without pushing to private?
[04:15] Priya: built-in tracing and RBAC are available in Dedicated and Private; hosted can provide audit logs but longer retention and custom KMS tends to be enterprise/add-on. we do offer audit exports to your SIEM.
[04:26] Marcus: about egress costs, I need to confirm our cloud billing team — if we do Private VPC peering there will still be cross-region egress charges right? could be a blocker.
[04:35] Jordan: yes, egress is often overlooked. we'll list network patterns and typical egress implications in the pricing sheet so you can model it.
[04:42] Sofia: timeline — our leadership wants a pilot in 3 weeks and a decision by end of month. is that realistic?
[04:49] Priya: 3 weeks is tight but doable for a short benchmark pilot; we'll need prompt sets, a small sample of telemetry, and access (or you can upload). we'll produce a per-token breakdown and recommended hosting mix.
[05:01] [00:05:00] Jordan: let's dig into batching numbers — in our experience continuous batching windows of 50-200ms give most customers a 10-30% per-token reduction without hurting p99 too much. but at high concurrency you get better packing so diminishing returns.
[05:20] Rhea: do you have examples of how caching impacted cost for similar customers?
[05:24] Priya: yes, quick case: similar prefix-heavy forecasting customer saw effective token cost drop ~35% after prefix caching and small dedicated pool for realtime. note caveat: cache hit rates fluctuate by prompt variance.
[05:36] Evan: what about using quantized model variants for analytics to save money?
[05:40] Priya: absolutely. Redwood's Optimize suggests quantization levels for workloads: 8-bit or 4-bit variants for analytics (higher error tolerance) can cut per-token compute cost dramatically but you should evaluate QA. we recommend A/B tests to compare output quality.
[05:55] Marcus: security quick question: KMS integration — do we need to manage keys or can Redwood manage? we have strict policy to hold certain keys.
[06:02] Jordan: Redwood supports customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM for Dedicated and Private. Hosted can integrate with customer KMS for specific flows but there are limitations; we'll detail that.
[06:12] Luis: also adding that SSO/SAML and SCIM provisioning is supported for enterprise teams.
[06:18] Rhea: pricing items I care about: per-token for completion, per-embedding, reserved instance amortization, cache cost? do you bill cache separately?
[06:28] Priya: cache is bundled in dedicated reservations (not a separate line item usually), hosted may include cache tiers; embedding pricing is separate. our sheet will show per-token compute + overhead + any additional storage/ingress/egress assumptions.
[06:39] Evan: show us an example calculation for the two lanes (realtime vs analytics) with our numbers.
[06:44] Jordan: sure - realtime: 600 rph * avg 150 tokens = 90k tokens/hour, analytics: 9.4k rph * avg 200 tokens = 1.88M tokens/hour (again please confirm these numbers off call). if realtime sits on dedicated at X per-hour and analytics on hosted at Y per-token we can model burn.
[07:06] Rhea: I'm worried about burst tolerance — sometimes we have a 10x spike for grid events. will dedicated autoscale?
[07:14] Priya: Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling and burst capacity. you can set a baseline reserved pool and allow burst to hosted or fallback to quantized variants; routing policies handle it.
[07:25] Marcus: who owns network and infra ops for private deployment? us or Redwood?
[07:30] Jordan: Private is customer-hosted with Redwood control plane or optionally customer control plane; ops split depends on the chosen model. full on-prem means you own the infra, we ship the runtime and support. VPC deployment is hybrid.
[07:41] [00:30:00] Jordan: ok wrapping up, quick recap: Redwood will run a pilot benchmark with your prompt set, test batching configs and cache hit scenarios; we'll produce a pricing model showing hosted/dedicated/private tradeoffs and per-token math. Marcus will share VPC/firewall info.
[07:58] Evan: sounds good. can you also include competitor comparison? we ran a brief eval of OtherCloudAI and ModelServeCo and want to see where Redwood lands on latency and cost.
[08:07] Jordan: yes we'll include a high-level competitor snapshot (public info).
[08:11] Rhea: a note — we need p99 < 250ms for realtime, that is a hard SLO.
[08:17] Priya: we'll prioritize that in the dedicated baseline config for the pilot.
[08:21] Luis: and I'll add the egress modeling to the pricing sheet.
[08:25] Sofia: thanks all, will confirm prompt upload method in the follow-up.
[08:29] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll send notes and next steps within 48 hours.
[08:33] Evan: appreciate it, bye.

Meeting end.
